background: In November 2020, a collection of more than 23,000 allegedly breached websites known as Cit0day were made available for download on several hacking forums . The data consisted of 226M unique email address alongside password pairs, often represented as both password hashes and the cracked, plain text versions. Independent verification of the data established it contains many legitimate, previously undisclosed breaches. The data was provided to HIBP by dehashed.com .
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 226,883,414 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Passwords.
editorial: Twenty-three thousand websites. That number is the whole story, because almost none of them are sites you would remember using. The forum you joined once in 2013, the shop that sold one thing you needed, the local club, the game that shut down, small sites with small security budgets, breached individually and unremarkably, then swept into one collection. Nobody notified anyone.

Most of those sites never knew, and a good number no longer existed by the time the collection was published. There is no company here to be accountable, no disclosure statement, and no reset email coming. The compilation also carried cracked plain-text passwords alongside the hashes, which removes the last bit of friction.

If you find yourself in this one, the question is not which site leaked it, that is usually unanswerable, but where else that password was ever used. That is the only question this data makes it possible to act on.

fields.name: Passwords
fields.why: Anyone reusing this password elsewhere has those accounts exposed too, credential stuffing is automated and tries them all within days.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

actions: Change this password anywhere you reused it, starting with your email account, that is the one that can reset all the others.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
